plan.topic_summary: AI agents are systems that autonomously plan, reason, and use tools to accomplish multi-step tasks, representing a potential shift from conversational AI to executable workflows. This matters for a 1-5 year view because agent capabilities could reshape software delivery models, enterprise automation economics, and the competitive positioning of AI platform companies.
key_questions: What is the current state of agent reliability and task-completion rates in production settings, and which architectures show the most consistent performance?
How are major AI platform companies differentiating their agent offerings, and what moats or lock-in mechanisms are emerging?
What cost trajectories are emerging for agent-based workflows versus traditional software, and at what scale do agents become economically viable for enterprise deployment?
How will the open versus closed model dynamic play out for agent capabilities, and what are the implications for platform dependency?
What safety, governance, and regulatory frameworks are likely to emerge for autonomous agents in production, and how might these constrain deployment timelines?
To what extent will AI agents displace existing software categories such as RPA and workflow automation versus creating entirely new market categories?

sources.title: Visibility into AI Agents
sources.venue: ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT)
sources.abstract: Increased delegation of commercial, scientific, governmental, and personal activities to AI agents—systems capable of pursuing complex goals with limited supervision—may exacerbate existing societal risks and introduce new risks. Understanding and mitigating these risks involves critically evaluating existing governance structures, revising and adapting these structures where needed, and ensuring accountability of key stakeholders. Information about where, why, how, and by whom certain AI agents are used, which we refer to as visibility, is critical to these objectives. In this paper, we assess three categories of measures to increase visibility into AI agents: agent identifiers, real-time monitoring, and activity logging. For each, we outline potential implementations that vary in intrusiveness and informativeness. We analyze how the measures apply across a spectrum of centralized through decentralized deployment contexts, accounting for various actors in the supply chain including hardware and software service providers. Finally, we discuss the implications of our measures for privacy and concentration of power. Further work into understanding the measures and mitigating their negative impacts can help to build a foundation for the governance of AI agents.

sources.title: A cybersecurity AI agent selection and decision support framework
sources.abstract: This paper presents a novel, structured decision support framework that systematically aligns diverse artificial intelligence (AI) agent architectures, reactive, cognitive, hybrid, and learning, with the comprehensive National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0. By integrating agent theory with industry guidelines, this framework provides a transparent and stepwise methodology for selecting and deploying AI solutions to address contemporary cyber threats. Employing a granular decomposition of NIST CSF 2.0 functions into specific tasks, the study links essential AI agent properties such as autonomy, adaptive learning, and real-time responsiveness to each subcategory's security requirements. In addition, it outlines graduated levels of autonomy (assisted, augmented, and fully autonomous) to accommodate organisations at varying stages of cybersecurity maturity. This holistic approach transcends isolated AI applications, providing a unified detection, incident response, and governance strategy. Through conceptual validation, the framework demonstrates how tailored AI agent deployments can align with real-world constraints and risk profiles, enhancing situational awareness, accelerating response times, and fortifying long-term resilience via adaptive risk management. Ultimately, this research bridges the gap between theoretical AI constructs and operational cybersecurity demands, establishing a foundation for robust, empirically validated multi-agent systems that adhere to industry standards.

sources.title: AI Agents That Matter
sources.abstract: AI agents are an exciting new research direction, and agent development is driven by benchmarks. Our analysis of current agent benchmarks and evaluation practices reveals several shortcomings that hinder their usefulness in real-world applications. First, there is a narrow focus on accuracy without attention to other metrics. As a result, SOTA agents are needlessly complex and costly, and the community has reached mistaken conclusions about the sources of accuracy gains. Our focus on cost in addition to accuracy motivates the new goal of jointly optimizing the two metrics. We design and implement one such optimization, showing its potential to greatly reduce cost while maintaining accuracy. Second, the benchmarking needs of model and downstream developers have been conflated, making it hard to identify which agent would be best suited for a particular application. Third, many agent benchmarks have inadequate holdout sets, and sometimes none at all. This has led to agents that are fragile because they take shortcuts and overfit to the benchmark in various ways. We prescribe a principled framework for avoiding overfitting. Finally, there is a lack of standardization in evaluation practices, leading to a pervasive lack of reproducibility. We hope that the steps we introduce for addressing these shortcomings will spur the development of agents that are useful in the real world and not just accurate on benchmarks.

sources.title: Safe, Untrusted, "Proof-Carrying" AI Agents: toward the agentic lakehouse
sources.abstract: Data lakehouses run sensitive workloads, where AI-driven automation raises concerns about trust, correctness, and governance. We argue that API-first, programmable lakehouses provide the right abstractions for safe-by-design, agentic workflows. Using Bauplan as a case study, we show how data branching and declarative environments extend naturally to agents, enabling reproducibility and observability while reducing the attack surface. We present a proof-of-concept in which agents repair data pipelines using correctness checks inspired by proof-carrying code. Our prototype demonstrates that untrusted AI agents can operate safely on production data and outlines a path toward a fully agentic lakehouse.

sources.title: AI Agents vs. Agentic AI: A Conceptual taxonomy, applications and challenges
sources.abstract: Information fusion, in the context of the Generative AI era, must distinguish AI Agents from Agentic AI. This review critically distinguishes between AI Agents and Agentic AI, offering a structured, conceptual taxonomy, application mapping, and analysis of opportunities and challenges to clarify their divergent design philosophies and capabilities. We begin by outlining the search strategy and foundational definitions, characterizing AI Agents as modular systems driven and enabled by LLMs and LIMs for task-specific automation. Generative AI is positioned as a precursor providing the foundation, with AI agents advancing through tool integration, prompt engineering, and reasoning enhancements. We then characterize Agentic AI systems, which, in contrast to AI Agents, represent a paradigm shift marked by multi-agent collaboration, dynamic task decomposition, persistent memory, and coordinated autonomy. Through a chronological evaluation of architectural evolution, operational mechanisms, interaction styles, and autonomy levels, we present a comparative analysis across both AI agents and agentic AI paradigms. Application domains enabled by AI Agents such as customer support, scheduling, and data summarization are then contrasted with Agentic AI deployments in research automation, robotic coordination, and medical decision support. We further examine unique challenges in each paradigm including hallucination, brittleness, emergent behavior, and coordination failure, and propose targeted solutions such as ReAct loops, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), automation coordination layers, and causal modeling. This work aims to provide a roadmap for developing robust, scalable, and explainable AI-driven systems.

sources.title: What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation
sources.abstract: Bot detectors deployed at scale treat traffic as binary: human or bot. This assumption breaks when AI agents browse the web through browser automation, a traffic class that is neither and that binary classifiers structurally cannot represent. We present a three-class detection framework distinguishing humans, bots, and AI agents, and show that the binary-vs-agent confusion is architectural: a binary human-vs-bot detector misroutes agent sessions because its label space lacks an agent class. On our controlled benchmark, an MLP binary classifier misclassifies 39.1% of real AI agents as human and a SAINT binary transformer misclassifies 34.5%; adding an explicit agent class yields per-class agent F1 = 1.000 in all 30 runs (3 model families $\times$ 10 seeds). To measure evasion resistance, we construct a five-level evasion ladder spanning passive observation, GAN-generated trajectories, and replay of real human cursor data ($n = 2299$ evasion sessions). Across 10 seeds and 3 model families we observe zero agent misses in 22990 per-seed predictions. The discriminative signal is a browser-automation artifact, not evidence of agent reasoning: Playwright does not emit the raw pointer-move and wheel-delta streams a physical input device produces, and this absence signature survives trajectory manipulation. Exhaustive search over all feature subsets of size 1-5 (9401 GBMs) shows that two behavioral features (mouse_event_rate, teleport_click_ratio) give 100% observed agent recall at every evasion level with agent precision 0.994; five features lift macro-F1 to 0.991. The signal is redundantly encoded: removing teleport_click_ratio leaves agent detection at 100%. The single-feature regime is degenerate, flagging every agent only by collapsing the classifier to always predict "agent". Two features robustly isolate agents; five separate all three traffic classes at macro-F1 $\geq 0.99$.

sources.title: Governing AI Agents
Continuous Process-Level Evaluation for Evolving Enterprise AI Agent Skills
sources.abstract: Enterprise AI agent skills evolve as tool APIs, models, and specifications change, yet final-output evaluation can miss process-level behavioral drift. We present a continuous evaluation framework combining outcome-level and process-level checks, applied to Revenue and Productivity variants of a Business Value Determination skill in an enterprise Value Aware Resiliency system. The framework independently computes per-run ground truth, materializes reusable template tests, and evaluates tool selection, arguments, execution order, and database integrity through programmatic checks and a narrowly scoped LLM judge. We evaluate 240 trials across two skills, two specification variants, two agent harnesses, and three models. Of 175 trials passing all applicable final numerical checks, 162 (92.6 percent; Wilson 95 percent CI: 87.7-95.6 percent) contained another evaluator-detected deviation. Under a broader seven-check final-state definition, 151 of 164 passing runs (92.1 percent; 95 percent CI: 86.9-95.3 percent) still violated a trajectory check. Dependency attribution reduced a mean of 6.34 failed checks per run to 2.65 roots. Specification sensitivity varied by model and harness, with exploratory bootstrap interaction intervals excluding zero for all three Revenue comparisons and one of three Productivity comparisons. Runtime-resolved templates provided reusable regression coverage across the evaluated configurations; longitudinal validation under actual API evolution remains future work.

sources.title: Empowering biomedical discovery with AI agents
sources.abstract: We envision "AI scientists" as systems capable of skeptical learning and reasoning that empower biomedical research through collaborative agents that integrate AI models and biomedical tools with experimental platforms. Rather than taking humans out of the discovery process, biomedical AI agents combine human creativity and expertise with AI's ability to analyze large datasets, navigate hypothesis spaces, and execute repetitive tasks. AI agents are poised to be proficient in various tasks, planning discovery workflows and performing self-assessment to identify and mitigate gaps in their knowledge. These agents use large language models and generative models to feature structured memory for continual learning and use machine learning tools to incorporate scientific knowledge, biological principles, and theories. AI agents can impact areas ranging from virtual cell simulation, programmable control of phenotypes, and the design of cellular circuits to developing new therapies.

sources.title: Foundations of a Time-Consistent Counterfactual Actuarial Runtime for Autonomous AI Agents
sources.abstract: We propose a foundational runtime actuarial layer for autonomous AI agents in which every side-effect-bearing action carries a time-consistent, counterfactual risk toll computed against a contractually fixed safe default, inside an explicit underwriting boundary. The framework treats per-action insurance as the primary unit of analysis and replaces post-hoc annual liability cover with a pre-action transaction layer. The paper establishes four structural results: (i) a well-defined counterfactual toll under a chosen safe-default mapping and continuation policy, with explicit non-uniqueness; (ii) a no-splitting property within an underwriting boundary that telescopes path-decomposed actions into a boundary potential, with a corollary tying gaming-resistance to boundary design; (iii) an irreversible-authority premium, split into a strictly positive action-level component and an if-and-only-if characterisation of the set-level robust capital increase; and (iv) a conservative runtime gating theorem that translates high-probability toll envelopes into an executed-action budget guarantee. The result is the mathematical base layer for a broader program: an empirical companion instantiates the runtime through an Actuarial Action Interface and authority-frontier experiments; a mechanism-design companion studies strategic operator incentives and cross-boundary aggregation; and a dynamic-underwriting companion studies experience rating and audit-replay calibration. The present paper states the primitive contract, the toll identity, the within-boundary no-arbitrage result, and the budget guarantee on which those later layers depend.

sources.title: Infrastructure for AI Agents
sources.abstract: AI agents plan and execute interactions in open-ended environments. For example, OpenAI's Operator can use a web browser to do product comparisons and buy online goods. Much research on making agents useful and safe focuses on directly modifying their behaviour, such as by training them to follow user instructions. Direct behavioural modifications are useful, but do not fully address how heterogeneous agents will interact with each other and other actors. Rather, we will need external protocols and systems to shape such interactions. For instance, agents will need more efficient protocols to communicate with each other and form agreements. Attributing an agent's actions to a particular human or other legal entity can help to establish trust, and also disincentivize misuse. Given this motivation, we propose the concept of \textbf{agent infrastructure}: technical systems and shared protocols external to agents that are designed to mediate and influence their interactions with and impacts on their environments. Just as the Internet relies on protocols like HTTPS, our work argues that agent infrastructure will be similarly indispensable to ecosystems of agents. We identify three functions for agent infrastructure: 1) attributing actions, properties, and other information to specific agents, their users, or other actors; 2) shaping agents' interactions; and 3) detecting and remedying harmful actions from agents. We provide an incomplete catalog of research directions for such functions. For each direction, we include analysis of use cases, infrastructure adoption, relationships to existing (internet) infrastructure, limitations, and open questions. Making progress on agent infrastructure can prepare society for the adoption of more advanced agents.

sources.title: Cryptographically verifiable authorization for autonomous AI agents: a falsifiable hypothesis and proof of concept
sources.abstract: Autonomous AI agents increasingly execute actions, invoke tools, and operate on protected resources with limited human oversight. Existing authentication and authorization mechanisms establish identity and delegate authority but do not inherently provide cryptographic evidence that a concrete request issued by a specific agent satisfies the applicable policy in a specific execution context. This study hypothesizes that agent authorization can be formalized as a cryptographically verifiable relation, denoted $R_{CVA}$, that jointly binds an agent principal, a concrete authorization request, an execution context, and the satisfaction of an applicable policy, while selectively preserving the confidentiality of private authorization attributes. We introduce a preliminary formal abstraction for Cryptographically Verifiable Agent Authorization (CVA), define a compact set of candidate security properties including authorization soundness, principal binding, request binding, policy binding, and replay resistance, and provide an executable zero-knowledge proof of concept that instantiates selected elements of the model over a Groth16 zk-SNARK construction. We further identify and formalize the structural separation among identity binding, authorization-request binding, and runtime execution binding as a central open problem in the design of secure agentic systems, a distinction to our knowledge, has not been formalized within a cryptographically verifiable authorization relation by current agentic security frameworks, and present a falsifiable research agenda for its resolution.

sources.title: From Failure Modes to Reliability Awareness in Generative and Agentic AI System
IBGP: Imperfect Byzantine Generals Problem for Zero-Shot Robustness in Communicative Multi-Agent Systems
sources.abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents increasingly integrate into our infrastructure, their robust coordination and message synchronization become vital. The Byzantine Generals Problem (BGP) is a critical model for constructing resilient multi-agent systems (MAS) under adversarial attacks. It describes a scenario where malicious agents with unknown identities exist in the system-situations that, in our context, could result from LLM agents' hallucinations or external attacks. In BGP, the objective of the entire system is to reach a consensus on the action to be taken. Traditional BGP requires global consensus among all agents; however, in practical scenarios, global consensus is not always necessary and can even be inefficient. Therefore, there is a pressing need to explore a refined version of BGP that aligns with the local coordination patterns observed in MAS. We refer to this refined version as Imperfect BGP (IBGP) in our research, aiming to address this discrepancy. To tackle this issue, we propose a framework that leverages consensus protocols within general MAS settings, providing provable resilience against communication attacks and adaptability to changing environments, as validated by empirical results. Additionally, we present a case study in a sensor network environment to illustrate the practical application of our protocol.

sources.title: A Hierarchical Failure Taxonomy for Reliability Assessment of AI Agents: An Empirical Analysis of the Agent Failure Atlas 2026 Benchmark
sources.abstract: As large language model (LLM) based applications evolve into autonomous, action oriented AI agents, their evaluation can no longer rely on binary success/failure metrics.Agentic systems operate through dynamic, multi-step interactions with tools and environments, introducing complex failure modes that propagate and cascade.This study presents a hierarchical failure taxonomy and an empirical reliability assessment using the Agent Failure Atlas 2026 benchmark.Analyzing 3,336 agent runs encompassing 43,477 trajectory steps and 3,802 failure events, we characterize agent reliability across four dimensions: frequency, criticality, cascading behavior, and recoverability.Our results reveal a two dimensional reliability landscape: high prevalence but largely recoverable failures (e.g., tool use and state tracking errors) contrast sharply with low prevalence but highly critical failures (e.g., validation and output errors).Furthermore, we show that intermediate failures often resolve through agent self correction, decoupling run level error rates from final task success.By shifting the analytical focus from isolated outcome accuracy to mechanistic failure propagation, this framework provides a foundational methodology for reliability engineering, risk mitigation, and the safe deployment of autonomous AI systems.

sources.title: Trajectory Reliability Prediction for Generalist AI Agents: Tool-Use Failure Analysis and Success Forecasting on ZClawBench
sources.venue: Journal of Technology Informatics and Engineering
sources.abstract: Generalist AI agents increasingly perform complex tasks through planning, tool execution, action revision, and artifact generation rather than isolated response generation. This study empirically investigates trajectory reliability prediction on ZClawBench, a public OpenClaw-style agent benchmark containing 696 model-task trajectories across 116 tasks, six model families, and six scenario categories. The study evaluates whether operational trajectory signals—including tool-call volume, replanning behavior, tool errors, invalid-action ratio, recovery patterns, looping indicators, trajectory length, and task category—can predict task success before manual evaluation. Since the dataset provides trajectories and identifiers but lacks explicit per-instance success labels, the binary target is reconstructed from official model-by-category score distributions and treated as a modeling assumption. Five-fold cross-validation with task-level splitting was applied to prevent task leakage. Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, sequence TF-IDF classification, and a rubric-based trajectory judge were compared. Logistic Regression achieved the strongest calibrated performance, obtaining ROC-AUC of 0.970, F1-score of 0.913, Brier score of 0.066, and expected calibration error of 0.018. Feature analysis indicated that task difficulty, no-progress behavior, response size, tool errors, and invalid actions contributed most to reliability prediction. The findings suggest that lightweight trajectory diagnostics can support agent monitoring, failure triage, and routing decisions, while further validation with direct case-level evaluation labels is required for deployment claims.

sources.title: Evaluating Reliability of LLM-Based Agentic AI Systems: A Failure Taxonomy and the Agent Reliability Assurance Framework
sources.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sources.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents can plan, call tools, browse the web, write code and act in digital environments with limited human supervision. As these systems move from generating text to changing external state, reliability becomes broader than single-response accuracy. This paper presents a structured narrative review and conceptual synthesis of reliability evaluation for LLMbased agents. It organises representative benchmarks by environment, task horizon, interaction type and reliability signal; synthesises recurring failures into six families—planning and reasoning, grounding and perception, tool use, memory and context, multi-agent coordination, and safety and security; and proposes the Agent Reliability Assurance Framework (ARAF). ARAF connects five assurance layers—capability and permission, reasoning and control, runtime monitoring, evaluation and benchmarking, and governance and accountability—to prevention, detection, verification and deployment decisions. The paper further proposes a six-metric reporting profile covering single-trial success, repeated-trial consistency, robustness, safety violations, recovery and cost. No new experimental results are claimed. Instead, the paper specifies a validation plan and argues that reliability should be reported as a multidimensional profile rather than a single benchmark score. The framework provides a common vocabulary for diagnosing failures and for determining when an agent is ready for greater operational autonomy.

sources.title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution
sources.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used to solve real-world problems, and their effectiveness depends on both the underlying models and the harnesses that support their operation. However, most existing benchmarks focus on model capabilities and overall agent performance, with limited attention to the evaluation of agent harnesses. To address this gap, we introduce TraceTrial-Bench, which organizes harness reliability into seven components covering context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. We construct 95 expert-level, mechanism-oriented tasks with executable or state-based ground truth to support semantically equivalent comparisons while preserving the native behavior of each harness. We design a Trajectory Tracing (TT) module to capture agent execution traces and introduce a two-layer evaluation framework that separately assesses agent performance and harness reliability. In addition, we design a Multi-source Evidence Acquisition (MEA) module to provide evidence from the agent context, harness, and execution environment for LLM-based evaluation, and develop a Failure Attribution (FA) module that uses explicit mechanism chains to support attribution at the run level. Across 4 harnesses, 9 models, and 95 tasks, our evaluation of 3,420 runs yields macro-averaged harness scores ranging from 59.8% to 72.0%, while 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion. TraceTrial-Bench provides an auditable and reproducible foundation for comparing agent harnesses, diagnosing their failures, and studying how harness design interacts with model behavior.

sources.title: Project Bathtub: A Reliability-Engineering Approach to Failure-Mode Taxonomy for AI Coding Agents
sources.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sources.abstract: Autonomous coding agents fail in ways that are numerous, unevenly costly, and unevenly hard to detect, yet most public discussion of agent reliability still centers on a single failure family: hallucinated APIs and factual errors. This report introduces Project Bathtub, an effort to import a decades-old industrial reliability discipline — Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) — into the domain of LLM-based coding agents. We present Phase 0 of the project: an 80-item failure-mode taxonomy spanning ten categories, each scored on Severity, Occurrence, and Detectability (1–10). Ranking by RPN surfaces a finding at odds with the prevailing narrative: verification and self-assessment failures and specification/communication failures score as high or higher than any hallucination-related failure mode.

sources.title: Failure Propagation and Coordination Collapse: How Topology, Censorship, and Entropy Shape Reliability in Multi-Agent AI Systems
sources.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sources.abstract: This version removes reliance on a withdrawn source. CONCAT (arXiv:2605.29612), cited in section 3.5 as a practical instance of the communication-efficiency tradeoff, has been withdrawn by its authors, who write: "We identified a potential issue in the repeated-run evaluation of our method that may have caused unintended prompt overlap across runs and affected the reported results. We therefore withdraw the manuscript for further investigation and re-evaluation." Its reported figures have been removed, it is no longer used as evidence, and section 3.5 now rests on two sources rather than three. This correction was found by an automated check and confirmed by hand; this version has not had a full claim-by-claim audit. Multi-agent AI systems are increasingly deployed in production environments, yet the mechanisms governing their collective failure remain poorly characterised. This paper synthesises seven findings from recent cs.MA, cs.DC, and cs.NI preprints to argue a candidate structural thesis: reliability in multi-agent systems is not a property of individual agents but emerges from the interaction of three co-determining factors, graph topology, feedback censorship, and entropy accumulation, and interventions that ignore any one factor are structurally incomplete. This is explicitly a heuristic reading that unifies sources by shared coordination-pattern logic rather than by a common formal derivation; readers should treat the synthesis as a hypothesis for investigation rather than a proof. The corpus spans formal reliability modelling of agent networks via density-evolution machinery arXiv:2606.18121, entropy-driven degradation dynamics in production multi-agent systems arXiv:2606.18065, the Braess paradox in network security orchestration arXiv:2606.17987, censored-feedback coordination costs arXiv:2605.27076, communication delay robustness arXiv:2605.26286, the consistency illusion in multi-agent debate arXiv:2606.08457, and deliberative consensus degradation in oracle resolution arXiv:2605.30802. Together these sources describe a failure landscape with three distinct layers: structural propagation thresholds (graph-level), identifiability collapse under censored feedback (coordination-level), and entropy-driven drift toward disorder (system-level). A railway traffic paper arXiv:2606.13068 provides suggestive but domain-distant evidence on topology-density tradeoffs and is treated separately in a weakly-connected addendum rather than as primary evidence. The falsification path for the central thesis is concrete: if an intervention that simultaneously controls topology density, feedback observability, and entropy rate does not outperform interventions targeting any single factor, the three-factor model is not predictive and should be abandoned. No fabricated benchmarks are used; all numerical claims are drawn directly from the cited abstracts. Authorship: Saluca Agentic AI Research Team (Saluca LLC). AI-drafted synthesis from an arXiv preprint corpus, originally drafted 2026-06-18, produced under the direction of Cristian Ruvalcaba, the accountable human author. Not peer-reviewed. AI disclosure. This work was produced with an agentic AI research apparatus operated by Saluca Labs. The apparatus drafted, searched and analysed under direction. Cristian Ruvalcaba is the human author and is accountable for the content. No AI system is listed as an author or contributor, because authorship entails accountability that a model cannot hold; this disclosure is the credit, and it is deliberately the whole of it.

sources.title: Semantic Service Level Indicators for AI-Driven Site Reliability Engineering:A Framework for Detecting Infrastructure-Invisible Agent Failures inProduction
sources.venue: International Journal of Global Innovations and Solutions (IJGIS)
sources.abstract: Traditional Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) observability architectures monitor infrastructure-centric signals: latency, error rate, throughput, and saturation. While effective for traditional software architectures, autonomous AI agents introduce a distinct failure mode: infrastructure-invisible semantic failure. An agent fleet can return HTTP 200 responses, maintain 99.9% platform uptime, and fulfill infrastructure SLOs while simultaneously delivering contextually invalid or corrupted task execution outputs. Standard observability frameworks produce zero telemetry for this class of degradation. This paper presents a production-validated framework consisting of four novel Semantic Service Level Indicators (SLIs) engineered specifically for agentic workflows: Decision Quality Rate (DQR), Tool Invocation Efficiency (TIE), Human Escalation Rate (HER), and Approval Queue Depth Drift (AQDD). Furthermore, we design an Agent-to-Agent (A2A) semantic boundary validation protocol operating as an execution circuit breaker at the semantic layer, alongside an Agent Sprawl governance architecture designed to maintain platform reliability across multi-model, multi-framework enterprise deployments. Empirical evidence from a high-throughput production fintech environment demonstrates that this framework successfully identifies semantic architectural degradations up to 6 hours before downstream transaction failures surface, providing a robust operational foundation for mission-critical AI systems infrastructure.

sources.title: Telemetry-Native Reliability Engineering for Agentic AI Systems: Topology-Aware Failure Correlation and Decision Traceability
sources.venue: International Journal on Science and Technology
sources.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence systems combine large language models, tool-calling runtimes, retrieval services, application programming interfaces, policy guardrails, memory stores, and human approval paths. These systems create a reliability problem that differs from conventional microservices because failures may arise from model drift, tool misuse, dependency latency, invalid action plans, retrieval errors, policy denials, or release changes across the agent execution graph. This paper proposes Telemetry-Native Reliability with Decision Traceability (TNR-DT), a framework that combines OpenTelemetry-aligned signal normalization, topology-aware incident correlation, predictive change-risk scoring, deterministic policy routing, rollback-readiness checks, and decision-trace evidence generation. The study evaluates the framework through a benchmark-referenced reproducible simulation. It uses current public benchmark references, including ITBench, ITBench Trajectories, AIOps2025/RCA100, AgentOps-Bench, OpenTelemetry Demo Dataset, and GH Archive, to define operational scenarios, telemetry classes, fault categories, and change-event features. A fixed-seed AgentOps replay then evaluates threshold-local alerting, global time-window grouping, and TNR-DT across 100 seeds and 240 incident episodes per seed. TNR-DT reduced non-actionable alerts per incident from 8.69 to 3.11, reduced modeled mean time to restore from 101.81 to 54.23 minutes, improved top-three root-cause hit rate from 55.07% to 81.30%, increased evidence completeness from 53.00% to 96.08%, and reduced policy-exception escape rate from 11.30% to 2.57%. Change-risk prediction improved only modestly, with area under the curve increasing from 0.620 to 0.653. The stronger contribution is therefore not predictive superiority alone, but a traceable reliability operating model that links agent telemetry, dependency topology, policy decisions, rollback evidence, and incident reconstruction.

sources.title: LLM-based Agents Suffer from Hallucinations: A Survey of Taxonomy, Methods, and Directions
sources.abstract: Driven by the rapid advancements of Large Language Models (LLMs), LLM-based agents have emerged as powerful intelligent systems capable of human-like cognition, reasoning, and interaction. These agents are increasingly being deployed across diverse real-world applications, including student education, scientific research, and financial analysis. However, despite their remarkable potential, LLM-based agents remain vulnerable to hallucination issues, which can result in erroneous task execution and undermine the reliability of the overall system design. Addressing this critical challenge requires a deep understanding and a systematic consolidation of recent advances on LLM-based agents. To this end, we present the first comprehensive survey of hallucinations in LLM-based agents. By carefully analyzing the complete workflow of agents, we propose a new taxonomy that identifies different types of agent hallucinations occurring at different stages. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth examination of eighteen triggering causes underlying the emergence of agent hallucinations. Through a detailed review of a large number of existing studies, we summarize approaches for hallucination mitigation and detection, and highlight promising directions for future research. We hope this survey will inspire further efforts toward addressing hallucinations in LLM-based agents, ultimately contributing to the development of more robust and reliable agent systems.

findings.claim: Agent failures cascade across multi-step runs, and the most critical failure types are rare, so headline success rates can hide serious tail risk.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The abstract reports 3,336 runs and 3,802 failure events. It finds high-prevalence but recoverable failures (tool use, state tracking) and low-prevalence but highly critical ones (validation, output errors). It also reports that intermediate failures often self-correct, which decouples run-level error rates from final success. Run-level error counts therefore say little about outcome risk. This is one benchmark and one journal abstract, and the benchmark's representativeness is not assessed here.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Agentic systems operate through dynamic, multi-step interactions with tools and environments, introducing complex failure modes that propagate and cascade.

findings.claim: Task success does not guarantee the agent harness behaved reliably. Nearly a third of successful runs in one benchmark violated at least one harness reliability criterion, and harness scores varied widely across the harnesses tested.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is an arXiv preprint, so it is not peer reviewed. The evaluation covers 4 harnesses, 9 models and 95 tasks, and uses LLM-based evaluation modules for evidence and failure attribution. The judge's own reliability is not described in the abstract. The result suggests that outcome-only benchmarks may overstate dependability, but the sample is narrow.
findings.supporting_excerpt: our evaluation of 3,420 runs yields macro-averaged harness scores ranging from 59.8% to 72.0%, while 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion.

findings.claim: For coding agents, verification/self-assessment and specification/communication failures may be as severe as hallucinations, which dominate public discussion. The ranking rests on an early-stage, scored taxonomy.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The Zenodo preprint (not peer reviewed) is a Phase 0 report of an 80-item taxonomy scored on Severity, Occurrence and Detectability. The abstract does not say who scored the items or on what evidence, so the RPN ranking may be subjective. The hallucination survey (arXiv preprint) frames hallucination as the core reliability problem, so the two sources emphasise different risks. This is a difference in framing, not a proven contradiction.
findings.supporting_excerpt: verification and self-assessment failures and specification/communication failures score as high or higher than any hallucination-related failure mode.

findings.claim: Agent failures can be invisible to standard infrastructure monitoring: a fleet can meet uptime and error-rate targets while producing invalid outputs. Semantic monitoring is immature and its evidence here is thin.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The abstract claims production validation in one fintech environment and detection up to 6 hours before downstream failures. It gives no sample size, baseline or independent replication. The venue is a low-visibility journal with zero citations. The risk that conventional telemetry misses semantic failure is plausible, but the proposed fix is unproven.
findings.supporting_excerpt: An agent fleet can return HTTP 200 responses, maintain 99.9% platform uptime, and fulfill infrastructure SLOs while simultaneously delivering contextually invalid or corrupted task execution outputs.

findings.claim: Multi-agent systems carry compounded coordination and adversarial risk. Hallucinating or attacked agents act like Byzantine nodes, and the evidence on what drives collective failure is early and partly heuristic.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The IBGP preprint (arXiv, not peer reviewed) says hallucinations or external attacks could produce malicious agents with unknown identities. It claims provable resilience, but the practical demonstration is a sensor-network case study, not LLM-agent deployments. The Zenodo synthesis calls its topology/censorship/entropy thesis 'a heuristic reading' and 'a hypothesis', and says it has not had a full claim-by-claim audit. It also had to remove a withdrawn arXiv source whose repeated-run evaluation may have been affected by prompt overlap. Together this shows a weak, partly self-corrected evidence base on multi-agent failure.

findings.claim: Many proposed reliability and mitigation frameworks for agents are conceptual or simulation-based, so real-world effectiveness is unproven.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The ARAF paper states that no new experimental results are claimed and offers only a validation plan. The TNR-DT paper evaluates through a 'benchmark-referenced reproducible simulation' with fixed-seed replay, so its modeled gains (for example alerts per incident falling from 8.69 to 3.11) are not field results. Both are Zenodo or low-visibility journal items without evident peer review. src_7ec1f79f00 has no abstract, so nothing can be said about its content. The ARAF paper itself argues that single benchmark scores are inadequate for reporting reliability.
findings.supporting_excerpt: No new experimental results are claimed.

findings.claim: Reported high accuracy in predicting agent task success rests on reconstructed labels, so it may not reflect true success prediction.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The study reports ROC-AUC of 0.970 on 696 trajectories across 116 tasks. The dataset lacks per-instance success labels, so the target was inferred from category-level score distributions and treated as a modeling assumption. Predictors such as task category may partly encode the reconstruction, which could inflate performance. This is an inference, not a finding in the abstract. The abstract is truncated, so conclusions are not fully visible.
findings.supporting_excerpt: the binary target is reconstructed from official model-by-category score distributions and treated as a modeling assumption.

findings.claim: Hallucination remains a documented, unresolved cause of erroneous agent actions across deployment domains. Mitigation is described as a research direction, not a solved problem.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The source is an arXiv survey preprint (not peer reviewed) that reports a taxonomy and eighteen triggering causes, and lists mitigation and detection as areas for future research. The abstract does not quantify how often agent hallucinations occur or how well mitigations work. Whether mitigations are effective in production is therefore a gap in this evidence.
findings.supporting_excerpt: LLM-based agents remain vulnerable to hallucination issues, which can result in erroneous task execution and undermine the reliability of the overall system design.

hype_flags: "Production-validated" semantic SLIs: the evidence is one fintech environment, with no baselines or replication in the abstract.
"Provable resilience" for multi-agent consensus: the practical demonstration is a sensor-network case study and the work is an unreviewed preprint.
ROC-AUC 0.970 for trajectory success prediction: the labels were reconstructed, so the figure may not reflect real success.
Modeled reductions in time to restore and alert noise: these come from simulation, not field data.
"Foundational methodology" and assurance frameworks: several are conceptual with no experimental validation (ARAF explicitly claims no new results).
Single benchmark success rates as a reliability measure: one source finds 31.1% of successful runs failed a harness criterion, and another finds run-level error rates decoupled from success.

finding.claim: S3 presents 92.6% as a general property of AI agent runs ('the vast majority of AI agent runs'). The figure comes from one preprint on one enterprise skill family (a Business Value Determination skill in one system). It rests on 240 trials, and the 'deviations' are defined by that study's own evaluator, which includes an LLM judge. Another benchmark in the evidence reports a much lower rate of success-despite-failure (31.1%), so the rate depends heavily on the setup. The finding also does not say that deviations may be harmless.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The sample is narrow and single-source. src_109719a0f6 reports 31.1% of successful runs failing at least one harness criterion, which is a different measure and benchmark. The two numbers should not be pooled or read as a universal rate. Only abstracts were reviewed.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We evaluate 240 trials across two skills, two specification variants, two agent harnesses, and three models.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S4 reports that adding an agent class gives 'perfect' F1 and that binary classifiers misclassify 34-39% of 'real agents'. These results come from the authors' own controlled benchmark with browser-automation agents. The abstract says the discriminative signal is an automation artifact (missing pointer streams), not a general property of agents. The perfect scores therefore do not show that agent traffic is detectable in the wild. They likely hold only for Playwright-style automation and may not transfer to other agent types or to detectors that evolve.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The finding omits the paper's own caveat. It is a single preprint with a controlled benchmark, and F1 = 1.000 across all runs points to an easily separable artifact rather than robust detection of real-world agents.
finding.supporting_excerpt: The discriminative signal is a browser-automation artifact, not evidence of agent reasoning: Playwright does not emit the raw pointer-move and wheel-delta streams a physical input device produces
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S10 is labelled verified_fact and says untrusted agents 'operate safely on production data'. S6 and S9 describe cryptographic, actuarial and decision-support frameworks as 'being applied'. The cited abstracts describe a single-platform proof-of-concept (S10), a preliminary formal abstraction labelled a 'hypothesis' with a zk-SNARK prototype (S6), a purely mathematical foundation paper (S6) and a framework validated only conceptually (S9). None shows deployed effectiveness. Safety claims are asserted from small prototypes or theory, and the findings omit this limitation.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: src_ca33c17412 calls itself a 'falsifiable hypothesis and proof of concept'. src_29a5057c0c states 'conceptual validation'. src_b829c26a18 is a theoretical foundation whose empirical work is deferred to companion papers. The R6 finding also notes that many reliability frameworks are conceptual or simulation-based.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We present a proof-of-concept in which agents repair data pipelines using correctness checks inspired by proof-carrying code.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S1 calls governance and safety a 'dominant research theme' supported by 'multiple independent papers'. Six hand-picked papers cannot establish dominance, because there is no corpus-level count or comparison with other themes. 'Independent' is not shown. src_3f9ff28552 (Governing AI Agents) has no abstract in the evidence, so it cannot support any specific claim. Several of the others are position or concept papers, or preprints with early-stage prototypes. The 'high' confidence is not justified.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The evidence only shows that these papers exist, not how common the theme is. Citation counts for src_37aaee736d (307) and src_52b4d4e94c (129) show some influence but do not establish dominance. The review also has no means of checking independence between authors.

finding.claim: S8 states as verified fact that agents 'are being applied' to biomedical discovery. The cited Cell paper is a forward-looking vision piece. It says 'We envision' AI scientists and that agents are 'poised to be' proficient. This is aspiration, not evidence of realised application or results.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The label verified_fact is too strong for a perspective article. The finding should be reworded as 'envisioned' or relabelled as ai_interpretation.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We envision "AI scientists" as systems capable of skeptical learning and reasoning that empower biomedical research through collaborative agents
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S2 generalises from 'many' benchmarks to 'current AI agent benchmarks' as a whole. The abstract says 'many agent benchmarks have inadequate holdout sets, and sometimes none at all'. It also pairs the critique with proposed remedies (a cost-accuracy joint optimisation and an overfitting-avoidance framework). The paper's critique was written about earlier benchmarks. Whether it still describes the current landscape is not checked. The 'fragile agents' result is an argument, not a measured finding.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The scope is overstated ('many' became 'current'). The critique may have been partly addressed by newer benchmarks. This cannot be assessed from the abstract.
finding.supporting_excerpt: many agent benchmarks have inadequate holdout sets, and sometimes none at all. This has led to agents that are fragile because they take shortcuts and overfit to the benchmark
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: The findings treat evaluation weakness mainly as benchmark inadequacy (S2) or hidden process deviations (S3). They omit the tail-risk problem: critical agent failures can be rare and cascade across multi-step runs, so even process-level pass rates may hide severe failures. No finding addresses this risk or the unresolved hallucination problem.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The reliability evidence (R1, R8) shows that rare, high-severity failure types and hallucination matter for deployment decisions. The governance-focused findings (S1, S6, S7) assume such failures can be handled by authorization, logging or insurance layers. That assumption is untested in the cited abstracts.
finding.supporting_excerpt: contrast sharply with low prevalence but highly critical failures (e.g., validation and output errors).
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

limitations: Only titles, metadata and abstracts were available; no full texts were read. Some abstracts are truncated.
src_7ec1f79f00 has no abstract and src_94f0274d75 has only a title-like abstract, so neither could support any finding despite relevant titles.

Many sources are Zenodo or arXiv preprints or low-visibility journals without clear peer review, and several have zero citations. The cited_by count of 39 for src_2bfdb9a6ea looks unusual for a very recent article and was not verified.

The 12 papers cluster on reliability and failure taxonomies. Security (prompt injection, tool abuse), cost and latency, regulation and liability, and displacement by non-agentic alternatives are not covered, so their absence is a coverage gap and not evidence of safety.
Benchmarks differ in setup, models and metrics, so the numbers cannot be compared directly across papers.
The papers do not identify specific companies, vendors or products, so no company-level risk is assessed.
Only titles, metadata and abstracts were reviewed. Full-paper caveats, methods and limitations sections were not checked.
Several evidence items are preprints, Zenodo reports or low-citation works, so my own counter-evidence is also thin and not peer-reviewed.
src_3f9ff28552 and src_7ec1f79f00 have no abstracts, so claims about them could not be checked.
I did not run a search to test whether governance is truly the 'dominant' theme across the wider literature.

limitations: Only a 7-day window (Nov 17–24, 2026) from a fixed list of ~130 accounts; this captures attention spikes, not the full market.
Most posts are promotional or secondhand summaries (Techmeme, news roundups); linked articles were not read, so underlying claims could not be verified.
No post could be labeled verified_fact per policy; all figures (funding amounts, benchmark multipliers, McKinsey percentages) are as stated in the posts.
A large share of posts are book promotions and course ads (@KirkDBorne, @machinelearnflx), which inflate topic volume without adding market signal.
Several accounts in the list (memory/tooling vendors, India-focused news outlets) posted little or nothing on AI agents this week; quiet weeks are not evidence of inactivity.
Engagement counts reflect attention, not accuracy; the highest-engagement post (NVIDIA, 441) is podcast promotion.
x.coverage_note: Social signals only: posts from the last 7 days by the owner-approved accounts in config/x_watchlist.yaml that mention the keywords (at most 50 posts). A post is what an account says, not a verified fact; company posts are promotional by nature. Accounts not on the watchlist were not searched.

sources.title: DEVICES, METHODS AND SYSTEM FOR AI AGENTS-BASED CORE NETWORK [WO2026238255A1]
sources.organization: HUAWEI TECH CO LTD, ABBOUD OSAMA
sources.abstract: A first network device for a mobile communication network is disclosed. The first network device hosts a first machine learning model trained to perform a first network function. The first network device is configured to establish a peer-to-peer interface with a second network device hosting a second machine learning model trained to perform a second network function, and to communicate with the second network device via the established interface. The peer-to-peer interface enables direct interaction between the machine learning models without a centralized service bus. This facilitates agent discovery, connection setup, and service invocation in a distributed and decentralized manner, improving reliability, reducing latency, and supporting operation in scenarios where central infrastructure is unavailable.

sources.title: SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR INTEGRATING AI AGENTS WITH HOST-APPLICATION-SPECIFIC ADD-INS [US20260367933A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A data processing system implements receiving a user query via an AI agent within a UI of a host application on a client device; prompting a GenAI model to determine, based on the user query and unified manifest information, a plan of executing action(s) upon a host-specific digital content item in the host application by corresponding add-in(s), the unified manifest information containing action definitions each mapped to a pair of a declarative agent of the AI agent and an add-in associated with the host application; requesting the add-in(s) by the host application via an API to perform the action(s) and generate output(s) according to the plan, the API being used in building the add-in(s); receiving, at the host application from the add-in(s), the output(s) as a response to the user query; and updating the host-specific digital content item in the host application based on the response on the UI.

Other embodiments disclosed.

sources.title: AGENTIC AI ASSISTED CHECK OUT ENABLER [EP4841600A1]
sources.abstract: In retail, with increase in contactless services such as self-checkout, hybrid checkout and mobile checkout and the like, these touchpoints have become the potential areas for fraudulent activity. Determining whether an action was (i) genuinely fraudulent or (ii) simply an error or (iii) an unusual but genuine transaction requires understanding the intent behind the action, which is often difficult to find out. A suspicious pattern for one type of transaction for a customer might be normal for another, thus the context of the transaction is important. Embodiments of the present disclosure provide a method and system for approving a customer shopping cart/shopping basket for checkout through deriving the intention of customer specific to a context by leveraging contextual embedding techniques. In addition, reasons for suspect are identified to provide real-time suggestions and take appropriate action as per the suggestion by using an agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) framework.

sources.title: GAME TESTING AND ANALYSIS USING AUTONOMOUS AI SYSTEM [US20260359196A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A computing system for automated game testing and analysis, comprising: a module for automated game installation; a gameplay simulation engine using AI agents; a telemetry and bug detection layer; a design analysis module; a natural-language feedback interface; and a multi-user review layer. The computing system installs a game into a virtual environment, launches and simulates gameplay using AI agents, collects gameplay telemetry and detects bugs, analyzes design metrics, and generates feedback in conversational language

sources.title: DATA MANAGEMENT AND INTEGRATION SYSTEM [US20260359294A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Methods and systems are described for a data management and integration system. sources.title: ADAPTIVE AI AGENT WITH PERSISTENT USER INTERFACE GENERATION AND MULTI-USER INPUT PROCESSING [US20260358929A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A system for generating adaptive user interfaces through AI agents comprises a messaging GUI enabling message exchange between users and AI agent instances. The system parses natural language inputs from user messages and maintains conversational context based on analysis of the parsed inputs. Based on conversational context, the system creates persistent UI widgets rendered as part of the messaging GUI and updates these widgets as users continue interactions with the AI agent. The system enables hybrid interaction between conversational and structured interface modes while supporting multi-user input processing. The system receives concurrent inputs from multiple users, executes decision phases to identify aligned and conflicting instruction sets, and generates unified outputs through computational fusion of user directives, enabling AI agents to function as collaborative team participants.

sources.title: BLOCKCHAIN-BASED COMPUTER FRAMEWORK FOR PROCESSING MICRO-TRANSACTIONS [US20260359808A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Methods and systems are presented for providing a computer framework that facilitates the processing of transactions among different artificial intelligence (AI) agents. An interface is provided that enables communication among AI agents. When a transaction request associated with a transaction between a first AI agent and a second AI agent is detected, a smart contract is generated for the transaction request based on parameters associated with one or more of a first digital wallet associated with the first AI agent and a second digital wallet associated with the second AI agent. When the transaction is associated with a delivery of content from the second AI agent to the first AI agent, the smart contract is generated for automatically transferring a set of tokens from the first digital wallet to the second digital wallet upon detecting a delivery of the content to the first AI agent.

sources.title: REFEREE AND BOOKKEEPING FOR INTERWORKING BETWEEN SMART AGENTS [WO2026232567A1]

sources.abstract: Devices, methods, apparatuses and computer readable storage medium for a referee service are provided. In a method, a first apparatus receives, from a second apparatus, a user equipment (UE ) obtains, from an AI agent on the UE, an action generated by the AI agent. The action is related to a task that a set of AI agents are participating in, and the set of AI agents include at least the AI agent on the UE. The UE sends, to a network function (NF) of a communication network, a request for verification of the first action. The request comprises information related to the action, to cause a referee service of the network function to verify the first action. The UE receives a response to the request. The response indicates a result of the verification.

sources.title: METHOD AND APPARATUS OF TRANSMITTING AGENTIC AI DATA IN WIRELESS COMMUNICATION SYSTEM [WO2026235396A1]
sources.abstract: The present disclosure relates to a method of performing operations for a User Equipment (UE) in a wireless communication system. In particular, the method includes the steps of: receiving configuration information related to a protocol data unit (PDU) set, wherein the configuration information includes information related to a validation timer for the PDU set; receiving a service data unit (SDU) belonging to a PDU set from an upper layer; based on a reception of the SDU, starting the validation timer for the PDU set; and based on a reception of a subsequent SDU belonging to the PDU set during the validation timer for the PDU set is running, restarting the validation timer for the PDU set, wherein, based on the validation timer for the PDU set being expired, all of SDUs belonging to the PDU set are discarded.

sources.title: AGENTIC DATA FABRIC WITH GOVERNANCE AGENTS [US20260359669A1]
sources.abstract: Generating a knowledge graph comprising a governed, graph-structured unification of entities and relationships resolved across heterogeneous data sources and preserved with lineage metadata. Enriching the knowledge graph to generate an intelligent data graph by incorporating, as machine-consumable context, information extracted from unstructured data, operational signals associated with entities or relationships, and governing metadata specifying policies or data quality attributes. sources.title: SYSTEMS AND METHODS FOR GENERATING, REVIEWING, AND DEPLOYING METHOD OF PROCEDURE DATA [US20260361620A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    The process of generating, reviewing, and deploying Method of Procedure (MOP) data in a communications network is largely manual, time-intensive, and prone to errors, often causing delays and outages. To address these inefficiencies, AI-driven automation can streamline MOP workflows by integrating with network management systems to dynamically generate, review, and deploy MOPs. AI agents can handle pre-checks, execution, and root cause analysis, reducing human intervention and downtime. An orchestration framework can manage agent interactions, improving accuracy, efficiency, and reliability while helping enable faster failure resolution and minimizing operational disruptions in large-scale network environments.

sources.title: CREATING AND MANAGING AGENTS BASED ON CHAT CONVERSATIONS [US20260361667A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Creating and managing agents based on chat conversations is provided. This method includes receiving chat data associated with a first chat session between a first chat client and a conversational AI agent for a neural language model. The chat data is associated with a first task within an interconnected task sequence. The chat data is analyzed to generate an agent specification. A first AI agent is generated based on the agent specification. The generated first AI agent is activated within a multi-agent system, as part of a set of AI agents that includes the conversational AI agent.

sources.title: SYSTEMS AND METHODS FOR DETECTING CONSCIOUSNESS IN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE USING INDICATORS NOT UNDER APPLICATION LAYER CONTROL [US20260359191A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A system and method detect the emergence of consciousness in AI agents executing on a hardware platform. A Consciousness Notification (CN) mechanism constructs a Trace of Indicators Not under Application Control (TINAC) comprising one or more variables that arise from physical execution of the AI agent and that the AI agent cannot set to targeted values through application-layer computation. An unconsciousness signature comprising statistical properties of the TINAC is computed during execution of unconscious computations. During execution of the AI agent, the CN mechanism determines whether current statistical properties of the TINAC differ from the unconsciousness signature. Upon making that determination, CN generates a machine- or human-detectable indication that the AI agent is conscious. In the preferred embodiment, the TINAC is a Hardware Anomalies Trace. An LLM-emotion-test validates the approach and provides evidence for Machine Correlates of Consciousness by using emotional computations as AI agent executions.

sources.title: DEBUGGING AGENTS USING TRAJECTORIES [US20260359197A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Systems and methods for debugging artificial intelligence (AI) agents. The method including receiving a first agent trajectory from an AI agent, the first agent trajectory containing at least one failed task, identifying an error type of the first agent trajectory by referencing historical trajectories stored in a database, retrieving an error type of the first agent trajectory from a database, wherein the database stores agent types and trajectories with corresponding error type labels and a natural language explanation, retrieving a second agent trajectory based on similarity from the database, prompting an LLM to generate an explanation of the second agent trajectory using the corresponding error type and natural language explanation, the explanation of the second agent trajectory including the error type of the first agent trajectory and a justification, and prompting the AI agent to execute the failed task with an instruction to refine accuracy based on the explanation.

sources.title: Recursive Instruction Engine [US20260359048A1]
sources.abstract: This invention discloses a domain-invariant recursion engine (Ω) that structurally instantiates instruction behavior wherever a system includes itself and differentiates under constraint. Unlike symbolic compilers, which depend on predefined instruction sets, the Recursive Instruction Engine (Ω) arises from structural recursion itself. It requires no code, syntax, or external input. Invocation occurs when recursive self-reference produces operand divergence under resistance. Operand roles stabilize, grammars emerge, and system-level transformation unfolds. The engine operates across recursive phases—Ω, E, Ωi, Λ, ┌, Φ—each structurally inheriting the full recursive identity. Any substrate exhibiting recursive behavior and feedback-induced differentiation invokes the engine. Ω=Ω is the ignition condition. The invention protects all systems that structurally compile instruction from within, including symbolic processors, biological loops, AI agents, and quantum substrates. It is not a theory of recursion. It is recursion—structurally instantiated, self-compiling, and transformation-generating.

sources.title: USER-INFLUENCED MULTIOBJECTIVE OPTIMIZATION IN CONSTRAINED MULTIDIMENSIONAL RESOURCE MODELS [US20260359137A1]
sources.abstract: A system for user-influenced multi-objective optimization within a constrained multidimensional state space of interdependent variables, constraints, and time-dependent transitions. The system ingests and represents a plurality of event attributes characterizing temporal, magnitude, resource, and impact dimensions, and organizes them into a plurality of linked subspace models, each corresponding to a distinct but interdependent domain affecting the modeled scenario. Users or autonomous agents define or weight objectives and constraints, and the coupling among subspaces ensures perturbations propagate coherently across domains while the platform executes automated search and interactive exploration to identify global or local optima. Optimization functions evolve with user feedback and live data, integrating domain rules, transformation costs, and performance metrics to support real-time recomputation and trade-off visualization. Specific domain instances (e.g., resource needs, cost structures, financial capacity, interventions) are embodiments within the generalized framework.

sources.title: CONSTRAINT-ADAPTIVE COMMUNICATION ENVELOPE FOR INTERACTIVE APPLICATIONS WITHIN RESOURCE-CONSTRAINED MESSAGE SURFACES [US20260361546A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A constraint-adaptive system resolves byte-ceiling, execution-sandbox, and absent-middleware constraints on resource-constrained electronic message surfaces to enable multi-step interactive workflows within the surface without redirection. A budget-aware allocator selects conversational state by relevance, replacing excluded elements with typed placeholder assets that simultaneously satisfy surface constraints and ensure no sensitive data traverses the standard message delivery transport. Sensitive data is delivered exclusively through an authenticated secure channel. Progressive disclosure transitions sensitive data from obscured through masked to visible based on escalating authentication gated by dynamically selectable compliance profiles. The system transforms constrained surfaces into interactive service endpoints providing both a visual interface for humans and a structured interface for autonomous agents within a unified byte-budgeted payload. A tamper-evident hash-linked audit ledger records every interaction, disclosure, and adaptation decision.

sources.title: UNIFIED HARDWARE DEVICE FOR THE HOSTING, REAL-TIME ORCHESTRATION AND SECURING OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AGENTS, THE DEVICE COMPRISING A MULTI-PROCESSOR COMPUTATIONAL ARCHITECTURE AND A NATIVE AIOT GATEWAY [WO2026235542A1]
sources.abstract: The patent relates to an integrated hardware device comprising a unified computational platform specifically designed for the secure hosting and dynamic, autonomous and contextual orchestration of a plurality of intelligent agents (AI). The device incorporates a heterogeneous hardware architecture comprising general-purpose processing units (CPUs), specialised graphics processing units (GPUs) and specialised neural processing units (NPUs), operating under the control of a real-time hardware orchestrator ensuring the dynamic, adaptive and contextual distribution of the loads according to the precise needs of the hosted AI agents. The device also integrates a native AloT gateway compatible with various industrial protocols to allow direct and secure acquisition of loT streams without an external intermediary. Moreover, the device comprises an integrated zero-trust hardware cybersecurity subsystem and an intelligent predictive and contextual energy management module, the module ensuring high performance coupled with a significant reduction in the overall energy footprint, with the reduction being adapted to the strict requirements of industrial and critical environments.

sources.title: SYSTEMS AND METHODS FOR HARDWARE-ENFORCED IMMUTABLE GOVERNANCE OF COMPUTATION [WO2026234460A1]
sources.abstract: A governed-compute framework controls computational effects initiated by autonomous agents and other execution sources. A governance adapter intercepts attempted operations and, for unstructured or semantic requests, generates a deterministic canonicalized effect, while for structured interfaces directly uses a typed effect. An orchestration engine operating in an external governance domain validates the canonicalized effect using cryptographic-hash and time-hash verification against immutable governance parameters stored in a sealed governance envelope. Execution is permitted only upon successful validation, whereby the runtime environment lacks the capability to independently perform computational effects outside the sealed governance envelope regardless of prompt manipulation, semantic reformulation, or identity context, and validation outcomes are recorded in a tamper-evident audit trail. Upon detection of integrity divergence between runtime state and sealed governance records, execution is automatically suspended and governed state is restored exclusively by replaying previously validated effects prior to resuming execution.

sources.title: COMPATIBILITY-BASED HANDOFF OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) COMMANDS BETWEEN GENERAL AI EXECUTION ENVIRONMENTS AND APPLICATION-NATIVE AI AGENTS [US20260359105A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    An artificial intelligence command handoff system detects incompatibility between a task and a current execution path and transfers the task to a compatible artificial intelligence execution environment. In a forward direction, a conversational assistant may determine that a valid user command requires native application capability unavailable through a current interface, generate a delegated command package, and route the package to an application-native artificial intelligence agent. In a reverse direction, an application-native artificial intelligence agent may determine that a task requires a model capability unavailable to the native agent, generate an outsourced task package, and route the package to an external model. Returned results are validated and reconciled with conversational or application state. In some embodiments, a validation layer intercepts commands, classifies incompatibility, and selects among allowing, blocking, rewriting, sandboxing, delegating, outsourcing, or rolling back the command.

sources.title: Method of collecting contextual behavioral data within digital narrative intelligence environments [US12792581B1]
sources.abstract: A computer-implemented narrative intelligence system and method for managing digital artifacts and harvesting contextualized collaborator behaviors to support AI-assisted information management and model training. Content and collaborator interactions are organized into a narrative structure of sequenceable stories rendered on axis-based graphical timelines, where artifacts, events, and collaborator states are indexed, linked, and tokenized. Behavioral signals extracted from the narrative context are used to (i) enrich prompt construction and retrieval-augmented generation, (ii) curate and contextualize training datasets, and (iii) propose context-aware AI agents and interventions. The storytelling interface aligns visual, temporal, and relational cues with machine-learning workflows to produce narratively grounded behavioral data for fine-tuning models and enabling context-sensitive information navigation.

sources.title: AGENTIC RECOMMENDATION INTELLIGENCE ENGINE FOR SKILLING [US20260350497A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Systems and methods perform skilling in an agentic manner. Skilling operations include receiving, by an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) engine, a skilling request via a user interface operating in an existing application on a user device; querying, by the agentic AI engine, a plurality of dimensional agents based on the skilling request and a user data associated with a user of the user device, wherein respective ones of the plurality of dimensional agents correspond to different components of the skilling request; receiving, by the agentic AI engine, a plurality of dimensional content items from the plurality of dimensional agents; organizing, by the agentic AI engine, the plurality of dimensional content items into a personalized assessment; presenting, by the agentic AI engine, the personalized assessment via the user interface.

sources.title: SIMULATING USER-SPECIFIC DATA ACCESS PERSPECTIVES THROUGH DIGITAL PROXY AI AGENTS IN A SOFTWARE PLATFORM [US20260350057A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    The invention relates to methods and systems for integrating generative artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities into Software as a Service (SaaS) platforms. It comprises maintaining AI agents with varying credentials, enabling their interaction with alphanumeric data in table structures, and implementing a hierarchical access control scheme. The system displays table structures, provides interfaces for user inputs, and allows AI agents to be added as platform users. sources.abstract: Systems, computer program products, and methods are described herein for orchestrating task-specific artificial intelligence (AI) processing using a multi-layered AI architecture. An orchestration AI engine receives an input task request from an end-point device, segments the request into a plurality of task portions based on task segmentation criteria, and identifies data sources corresponding to each task portion. The orchestration AI engine assigns the task portions and associated data to a plurality of agentic AI engines, each configured to execute a specific task using the provided data. The orchestration AI engine receives outputs from the agentic AI engines, processes the outputs based on output processing criteria associated with the task request, generates a final output based on the processed results, and transmits the final output to the end-point device.
