draft.summary: Research and patent activity on AI agents is rising very fast: matching papers grew from 1,861 in 2024 to 8,813 in 2025 and are still accelerating this year, and patent publications grew from 39 to 139 over the same two years (code-computed counts, with recent years undercounted). Filings from several software vendors say they are shipping commercial agent products, and venture rounds were announced in the past week [M1, M2, M3, M4, X2]. The evidence for reliability, safety and customer results is much weaker. Several findings show that agent failures are hidden, rare but severe, or measured with unvalidated methods, and many proposed safeguards are prototypes or theory [R1, R2, R6, R8, C3]. Filings do not link R&D spend or revenue specifically to agents, and no customer-outcome data was provided [M10]. Large enterprises also list agents as a risk factor [M7]. The main uncertainty is whether current reliability can support wider autonomous use, and whether the surge in papers and patents reflects real commercial traction or hype around the topic.
draft.plain_summary: AI agents are software programs that can carry out multi-step tasks on their own, and many software companies say they are already selling them. Research and patent activity is growing very quickly, but the evidence that agents work reliably enough, and that customers are paying for them at scale, is still thin. The main thing that could stop the trend is agents making rare but serious mistakes that businesses cannot detect or control.

horizons.assessment: Hardware and memory vendors are marketing products at agentic workloads, and trade press is running an agentic-AI chip and system-design event. These are company claims and promotional signals, not evidence of purchases, and no supply-chain evidence is available.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Patent filings on orchestration, multi-agent coordination and agent-specific hardware show where applicants expect demand, but applications are claims and the hardware filing is a single applicant.

horizons.label: assumption
horizons.assessment: The cited evidence says nothing about whether agent-specific compute becomes a distinct market in 3-5 years.

bull.label: forecast
bull.narrative: Agent workloads, with many sequential calls and reused context, create sustained demand for tailored memory, networking and orchestration, which vendors are already targeting.

base.label: forecast
base.narrative: Agentic workloads are folded into general AI infrastructure demand, with vendors using the term in marketing but no clearly separate market emerging.

bear.label: forecast
bear.narrative: Slower agent adoption, or efficiency gains in software, reduce the incremental compute demand, leaving agent-specific hardware claims as marketing.

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Independent benchmarks or customer deployments confirming performance gains on agentic workloads.

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: Evidence comes from company posts and a single patent applicant, so it is promotional and unverified.

companies.label: unverified_claim
companies.name: Arm
companies.relevance: Claims, citing Signal65 research, that Microsoft's Arm-based Cobalt 200 delivers nearly 2x the agentic function-calling throughput of Cobalt 100. This is an unverified social-media claim.

companies.label: unverified_claim
companies.name: SK hynix
companies.relevance: Demonstrated MARS, CXL pooled memory sharing KV caches across servers so agents can reuse earlier work. Vendor marketing, not evidence of sales.

companies.label: unverified_claim
companies.name: ABA Tech
companies.relevance: Applicant for a unified hardware device for real-time agent orchestration; a patent application is a claim, and the company is not covered by the scout financials.

invalidation_conditions.label: forecast
invalidation_conditions.text: No measurable purchasing or deployment of agent-specific hardware appears in vendor filings.

conflicting_evidence.label: ai_interpretation
conflicting_evidence.text: Hardware-vendor emphasis on agentic workloads contrasts with documented reliability problems that could limit agent deployment volumes.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Code-computed counts show papers matching the topic phrases rising from 1,861 (2024) to 8,813 (2025), with the current year about 410% above the same point last year, so momentum is still building. The count uses exact phrases, is not normalised for publishing growth, and includes many preprints and position papers. The literature spans governance, evaluation and applications. Research activity is not commercial success.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Code-computed patent publications rose from 39 (2024) to 139 (2025), with 486 by 25 October 2026 versus 99 a year earlier. Filings cover orchestration, security/identity, application integration and domain uses. Absolute numbers are still modest, recent years are undercounted by publication delay, and applications are claims, not proof.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Vendors ship agent products, but evidence shows reliability gaps: failures cascade, critical failures are rare and can hide behind headline success rates, harness reliability varies, and hallucination is unresolved. Benchmarks are criticised, and some figures (92.6%) are strongly setup-dependent. Feasible in narrow supervised tasks; open for autonomous use.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Several listed software vendors say they have launched agent products, and one reports direct subscription monetisation. However, filings do not quantify agent revenue, and some descriptions are marketing language or plans.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Adoption evidence is mostly vendor statements about their own products or internal use, plus social-media signals clustered in customer service and workflow automation. There are no customer counts, usage or retention data in the findings; a company describing a product is not proof of adoption.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Vendors report large R&D budgets (e.g. Atlassian about 50% of revenue, Microsoft about USD 35.6B), though filings do not attribute them to agents. Several agent startups announced funding rounds in one week, including a USD 90M Series B. Together this indicates substantial investment, but attribution is indirect.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: The findings give no market-share or concentration data. Vendors describe changing competitive dynamics and disruption risk, and an analyst evaluation covered 17 contact-centre vendors, suggesting a crowded field, but that is not enough to rate a position.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Only promotional posts and one hardware patent application address hardware for agent workloads; no manufacturing, supplier or capacity evidence is provided, so no rating is possible.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Level 3 (elevated): products are shipping and first-wave adoption is claimed, but reliability, tail-failure risk and hallucination are unresolved, safety mechanisms are mostly prototypes, and revenue and customer outcomes are not shown. Large enterprises list agents as a risk factor. Related stocks are not stretched (moderate timing risk), so this does not push the level higher, though monday.com has high volatility. Challenges C1-C7 weaken several supporting findings.

missing_data: Agent-specific revenue, usage and customer outcomes from vendors (filings do not separate agent spending or revenue from other AI spending)
Independent, real-world failure rates and incident data for deployed agents (current figures come from single preprints with setup-dependent results)
Evidence that safety and governance proposals work outside prototypes
Market share and competitive concentration data
Supply-chain, manufacturing and capacity evidence for agent-oriented hardware
Patent assignee concentration and legal status of applications; most scout-named companies have only 1-2 patents
Regulatory and liability developments affecting autonomous agents
Verified sources for productivity claims (IBM and McKinsey figures are relayed social posts)
limitations: Findings are based on abstracts and short filing excerpts; headline and social-media items are unverified claims and carry little weight.
The research count depends on exact phrases and the surge may partly reflect relabelling and hype; the current year is partial and counts are not normalised for publishing growth.
Patent counts are undercounted for recent years because of publication delay, and applications are claims, not proof.
Several science findings were challenged by the Risk agent as over-generalised from single preprints, prototypes or vision papers.
Price and timing metrics cover about 100 trading days for four stocks only and are risk context, not a buy/sell signal.
Company Scout scores are a heuristic, and smaller companies carry more risk and less disclosure. This assessment is research, not investment advice, and makes no price targets or return forecasts.

notes: Weights are initial assumptions, not fitted to data. Score and confidence are explainable heuristics, not a validated prediction of stock performance; confidence is not a probability of profit.
Sources are de-duplicated by URL/DOI/title. A single announcement reported by several outlets is not yet merged into one event.
score.formula: score = sum(weight x rating/5) / sum(weight of evidenced dimensions) x 100 (risk does not reduce it). confidence = evidence confidence x (1 - 0.10 x risk rating), where evidence confidence combines evidence coverage, the confidence of the cited ratings and the share of verified facts. Dimensions without cited findings are 'missing', not zero.
